problem: Dialogue-based robot navigation systems ignore sociolinguistic cues such as politeness, so the robot cannot adapt its behaviour (speed, voice, posture) to a user's patience or impatience.
motivation: Impolite utterances may signal that the user is in a hurry, and polite ones a patient user, so a service robot in healthcare, retail or education should adapt its navigation and responses accordingly. Politeness is a cheap, linguistically detectable social cue for driving this adaptation.
key_idea: Detect the user's intention (dialogue act plus slots) and degree of politeness from speech, and use the cumulative politeness to modulate the Pepper robot's navigation speed, voice pitch, head pitch and LED colour during a guided tour.
insight: A modular dialogue system can map a discretized politeness score onto multiple robot social cues without changing the navigation stack. The paper offers no ablation or user study, so it shows feasibility only; the appropriateness of the behaviour mappings is explicitly left unvalidated.
method: Dialogue act recognition: a hierarchical RNN predicts the dialogue act, then slots, then slot values; it runs alongside the Snips NLU engine (deterministic plus probabilistic parser), with the two validating each other via confidence heuristics.
Politeness detection: an RNN trained on the Stanford Politeness Corpus and fine-tuned on scenario data; outputs a degree of politeness discretized to polite (1), neutral (0), impolite (-1).
Dialogue flow: a rule-based engine with a context queue that triggers acts such as FinishedOne and tracks Accept/Reject to move through the list of locations.
Response manager: selects pre-defined response templates by dialogue act and degree of politeness.
State manager: a valence/arousal-inspired model maps the cumulative sum of politeness to LED colour, head pitch, voice pitch and navigation speed.
Motion manager: teleoperation and scripted navigation via NAOqi moveToward/moveTo, plus ROS navigation (depth-to-laserscan, gmapping, AMCL, global and local costmaps) fed by a client-server API.

setting.backbone: RNNs (dialogue act, slots and politeness, trained from scratch or fine-tuned) + Snips NLU engine; rule-based dialogue flow
setting.training_data: Stanford Politeness Corpus plus a small self-created scenario-specific dialogue act/slot dataset
setting.observation: Speech converted to text by NAOqi ASR; Pepper depth image converted to virtual laser scan for SLAM and localization
setting.action_space: High-level goal locations sent to ROS navigation stack; NAOqi moveTo/moveToward; speed modulated by politeness
setting.privileged: Pre-built offline map of the environment (gmapping, post-processed); known department coordinates

numbers_note: No quantitative results; only qualitative plots of the robot internal state for polite vs impolite interactions.
results: The system was deployed on Pepper in a four-department lab tour. The robot slows down and spends more time with polite users and speeds up with impolite ones. No quantitative evaluation or user study was done.
limitations: No quantitative evaluation or user study; the appropriateness of the behaviour mappings is unvalidated
Rule-based dialogue flow, template responses and a small custom dataset in a single lab environment
Navigation is only to a few predefined named locations with a pre-built map, not language-grounded navigation
builds_on: Hierarchical RNN dialogue act recognition (Bothe et al.)
